newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU supports European Commission single market plan.
newsitem.headline: EU supports European Commission single market plan.

text.p: European Union internal market ministers gave their political blessing on Wednesday to an ambitious European Commission plan to plug holes in the bloc's single market by the launch of monetary union in 1999.
They discussed the outline plan put forward by the EU executive last month, giving suggestions as well as warnings on specific points but voicing general support for the initiative.

"In political terms this action plan, in the draft as it is on the table right now, has received complete support by the ministers," said Dutch European Affairs Minister Michael Patijn, who chaired the meeting.

EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti said he was "very encouraged" by the reception given by ministers to the single market plan, due to be finalised this month and then presented to EU leaders meeting in Amsterdam on June 16-17.
New British minister for European trade and competitiveness, Lord Simon of Highbury, hailed the Commission's draft as an "extremely well-worked paper".
"Trying to make the single market more effective is probably one of the key elements of our European policy," he told reporters. "This is a good draft action plan."
The European Commission, anxious to boost competitiveness and lower EU unemployment of around 11 percent, says a fully functioning single market is crucial for monetary union.

Despite the generally positive attitude of member states, however, several are sceptical about the action plan's short timetable in view of difficulties in the past to agree on controversial issues such as more tax harmonisation.

"A fixed and inflexible timetable does not serve the interests of the case," said Lorenz Schomerus, state secretary at the German economics ministry. "We have strongly recommended realism," he told reporters.
"Certainly it is hard to see that we could agree on all the new proposals by the January 1 1999 deadline," Britain's Simon said. Britain also had problems with the tax proposals, he said.

A Commission official conceded that many member states did not believe it was realistic to agree on all tax proposals by 1999, adding that Monti had never said the action plan would be fully achieved by that date.

A key target of the Commission's plan is for member states to apply and enforce properly existing single market rules, for example those affecting government contracts, which account for 11.5 percent of the EU's gross domestic product.

To step up pressure on offending member states, the Commission wants to publish regularly a "single market scoreboard" showing how well each country is complying with EU rules, including the number of complaints and infringement cases against it.

It also seeks to speed up infringement procedures against member states which violate single market rules, which today may take years. "Strengthened enforcement is of course part of the action plan," Monti said.
Wednesday's debate took place against the backdrop of new Commission statistics showing a slightly improving performance in implementing single market legislation at national level.

The Commission launched the single market programme in 1985 to create a huge domestic market to help European firms compete on world markets by removing all barriers to the free movement of goods, services, capital and people in the bloc.

Apart from the problem of enforcing existing rules, some single market proposals still await adoption by the EU, for example in the areas of company law, taxation, financial services and the free movement of people.
